Say who is calling, and answer or decline it by voice
no ticket
e526bfc · 10 files
Kevin: "i wanna know whos calling. right now only announces that theres a call. can i also pick it up or decline via voice?" Both yes. Three permissions, each verified against AOSP rather than assumed. WHY IT ONLY EVER SAID "A CALL" Not an oversight - the old code documented the limit and worked around it. TelephonyRegistry computes `r.canReadCallLog() ? phoneNumber : ""` on every callback delivery, so an app without READ_CALL_LOG is handed an EMPTY STRING, not null. LEGION held READ_PHONE_STATE only, so a generic line was the honest answer available. Now declared: READ_CALL_LOG (the only thing that delivers the number), READ_CONTACTS (number to name via PhoneLookup), ANSWER_PHONE_CALLS (an ordinary dangerous permission - TelecomServiceImpl checks it and its app-op and nothing else, so no dialer role is needed). READ_CALL_LOG is hard-restricted and would block a Play listing. LEGION is sideloaded and never listed, and adb install allowlists it by default. Written into the manifest so the day that changes, the constraint is already there. DO NOT migrate to TelephonyCallback.CallStateListener. Its onCallStateChanged has no number parameter at all - AOSP's dispatch comment says "The new callback does NOT provide the phone number" - so modernising off the deprecated PhoneStateListener would silently delete this feature. Said in the manifest and on the class. FOUR OUTCOMES, NONE OF THEM A GUESS CallerId resolves a contact name, a bare number, a genuinely withheld number, and "I am not allowed to look" - and keeps the last two apart. "I cannot see who is calling" and "the caller is unknown" are different claims, and collapsing them tells Kevin his caller withheld a number when the app was simply never permitted to check. Same shape as rendering a refused calendar permission as an empty day, which is settled decision 20. The announcement also stops offering what it cannot do: with no answer permission the prompt explicitly forbids offering to answer or decline. A BLOCKER FOUND BY TRACING, NOT BY TESTING isInCall was set true on RINGING, and LiveSessionController refuses to open a turn while isInCall - so the exact moment Kevin wants to say "answer it" was the moment the app showed "ON A CALL" and stopped listening. Voice answering was impossible before this and nothing would have reported that. Split into isRinging and isInCall: the proactive gate treats both as silence, the voice path deliberately does not. THE HONESTY PROBLEM acceptRingingCall() returns void. It reports nothing about whether the call was answered, so returning "probably fine" would push a lie one layer up into what the assistant says. CallActions instead WATCHES the phone's call state and reports what it observed: answering means RINGING became OFFHOOK. endCall does return a boolean and it is used, plus the same state check, because a true return is not the same as the ringing having stopped. That matters most for the case Android will not do at all: self-managed calls - WhatsApp, Signal, Teams - are silently ignored for a non-dialer app, with no error. The state check is what turns that silence into "that did not work, and here is why" instead of a confident false claim. Emergency calls cannot be ended either. Both named in the tool descriptions rather than discovered. Nine tests on the two describe() functions, which are the sentences that actually reach his ears. 1803 total, green. APK assembles, manifest merges. OWED on the phone: everything. Whether the number arrives, whether PhoneLookup matches his contacts, whether answering by voice beats the dialer UI to it, and whether the wake word can even be heard over a ringing phone - that last one is not addressed here and may well be the next problem. Both limits are written into the doc rather than left to be discovered - an unbooked conversation and a meeting that ran long are both invisible, and the 3-a-day cap carries what they miss. Both halves fail toward the notification. No calendar permission resolves to "unknown, so post it", never "free, so say it out loud" - the same unreadable-versus-empty split OpenerCalendarBriefing already makes, now a rule of the contract rather than a calendar detail. A raise that cannot be spoken is posted, on its own channel at IMPORTANCE_DEFAULT: quieter than reminders (which the user explicitly asked to be interrupted for), louder than the two silent service channels (a warning nobody sees is not a warning). Nothing anywhere claims a notification was seen - the channel is a kill switch Kevin can pull without the app knowing. Two refusals deliberately do NOT become a notification, and both would be wrong if they did. MutedByUser, because a kill switch that reroutes to the shade is not a kill switch. Suppressed, because he already brushed that exact rule off and posting it is the same nag through a different door. Quiet hours and the cap DO post - those mean "not out loud right now", not "you have heard enough of this". And I referenced R.drawable.ic_notification, which does not exist. All three existing notifications use the platform icon; this now matches rather than being the one that looks different for no reason. The reminder echo is closed. ReminderAlarmReceiver posted a notification AND spoke, unconditionally, for the same item in the same method. It now speaks first and posts only if the line was not said aloud. The raise opts out of the bus's generic notification via callerPostsItsOwnNotification, because a reminder already has a better one on the HIGH channel. That receiver is also the one place a caller overrides the bus's delivery judgement: it posts even for muted and suppressed, because a reminder the user explicitly set is not a nudge and must not be lost to a proactive mute, a declined nudge, or a spent budget. Second of six. Ticket 10's contract, ticket 02's hybrid, ticket 05's cap and quiet hours, ticket 08's register clause. ProactiveRaise replaces the bare String: ruleId, category, reason, facts, prompt. The gate refuses one whose facts are blank, which is the invented "lunch with Sam" caught structurally rather than by prompt wording. A convention with a comment was the cheaper option and was rejected because it is exactly what ticket 01 found had already failed once - three copies of one gate, two of which quietly diverged. Honest about its reach, in the class doc: the gate can check that facts are non-empty. It cannot check they are true, relevant, or complete. A silent failure becomes a refusable one; the prompt is not thereby correct. The gate now runs master, category, facts, suppression, quiet hours, cap, and returns a named RaiseOutcome rather than a boolean, so the delivery layer can tell "the user switched it off" from "over budget" - one of those deserves a notification and one does not. Quiet hours wrap midnight. `hour in 22 until 7` is an EMPTY range, so a naive window never fires and nothing looks broken; there is a test for it. Three spoken lines a day, Safety uncapped, counted from local midnight rather than a rolling 24h so last night's three cannot suppress this morning's first. PROACTIVE_CLAUSE sits at file scope beside CANNOT_CLAUSE, never per-persona - the trap ticket 08 named. One clause in it is load-bearing beyond taste: a goal nudge may name the goal, its deadline or its next step, and may never characterise how long it has gone untouched. Ticket 03 ruled the ignored-goal nudge permitted, so that sentence stands where a checkable rule would have. I introduced a regression and want it recorded as mine rather than as weather. Adding the switches put a Room read inside a gate that used to be pure, and ProactiveBusTest started failing with "Illegal connection pointer" - CarDatabase is a process-wide singleton while Robolectric resets its SQLite per test. The subagent that hit it reported it as pre-existing flake in code it had not touched. It was neither: ProactiveSettings.load was an hour old and speakIfAllowed did no database work before it. Fixed by splitting the arithmetic out as decideOnHistory, a pure function of values already fetched, and covering suppression/quiet-hours/cap there in plain JUnit. The pre-database checks are deliberately ordered first in speakIfAllowed so ProactiveBusTest can still reach them without Room. What that leaves untested is the WIRING - that speakIfAllowed passes the right rows in - and both test classes now say so rather than letting a green suite imply otherwise. The emit-on-success path went with it; that loss is written down too. ProactiveBusTest's "blocked while muted" was driving ProactivePreferences, which is a migration source now and gates nothing, so it had been passing for reasons unrelated to its name. It now exercises the master switch, plus new cases for a category-off raise and a factless one. Settings screen gains the five category rows. An empty category says "Nothing uses this yet." in words - not hidden, not greyed out. It stays toggleable, so turning Wellbeing on today gets its first nudge the day one is written. The row also stops hardcoding "Alfred", which CLAUDE.md sec 1 forbids and which I filed on ticket 12 - it takes companionName the way WakeWordRow already did. And the off-state copy now names safety explicitly: a kill switch whose description lists "openers, alerts, reminders" and omits the one category you would most expect to survive is not describing itself honestly. 1793 tests green. That distinction needed ProactivePreferences.hasStoredValue. isMuted cannot tell a fresh install from a deliberately-unmuted existing one - both read false - so the migration asks whether the key was ever WRITTEN. The absence of the value is the signal. Two things caught by checking rather than assuming: The hand-written migration had DEFAULT 0 and DEFAULT 'spoken' on two columns. Room does not turn a Kotlin constructor default into a column default, so the generated createSql has neither, and the identity hash would have disagreed on upgrade. CarDatabase.SCHEMA_VERSION was sitting at 26 while @Database said 27 - the v27 bump was forgotten before this change. Now 28. Play and add-to playlists by name against the driver's own library first
no ticket
be7e478 · 5 files
Ticket 08: `play_music`'s playlist type routed straight through public `/v1/search`, which is the wrong endpoint for "play my Roadtrip playlist" - search ranks the whole catalogue and its limit is capped at 10, so a hundred public playlists with similar names can bury the driver's own. SpotifyWebApi.myPlaylists() reads and caches `/me/playlists` (15-minute TTL, reasoning written into the code - long enough that a drive full of play/add requests costs at most one call, short enough that a freshly shared playlist shows up the same sitting). bestPlaylistMatch() fuzzy- matches the spoken name against that cache first (exact/containment/ Levenshtein tiers, all pure and unit-tested); only when nothing clears the threshold does resolvePlaylist() fall through to search, and play_music says so out loud when it does, naming what actually played. Each cached playlist carries a `readable` flag (owned by the account, or collaborative) per the research's hard boundary: `GET /playlists/{id}` only returns items for playlists the user owns or collaborates on, so a followed editorial playlist (Discover Weekly) is a real result the driver can still ask to play, but never one LEGION can write to. control_music gains `add_to_playlist` (POST /playlists/{id}/items - the /tracks -> /items migration the research called out), targeting the CURRENTLY PLAYING track, resolved through the library-only findMyPlaylist (never falls through to public search - adding to someone else's playlist was never what "add this to Roadtrip" meant). An unreadable match is named as unreadable before any write is attempted, never silently skipped and never reported as "no such playlist" - the exact case ticket 08 was filed to cover. No new tool declarations (ticket 03's one-net-new budget was already spent on get_music_queue): playlist-by-name folds into play_music's existing playlist type, and add_to_playlist folds into control_music's action enum alongside a new playlistName param. App Remote becomes the spine: it creates the device, not just plays on one
spotify-voice 02
66d1d4c · 4 files
Ticket 02 of the spotify-voice map. Implements the one play path every tool on this map funnels through (isInstalled -> ensureConnected -> ConnectApi.connectSwitchToLocalDevice() -> PlayerApi.play(uri)) instead of a bare play(uri) that assumed a device was already active. The switch-to-local step is what solves the cold case: asking for music with Spotify closed. App Remote's connect() alone creates an active device but doesn't say it's THIS phone; connectSwitchToLocalDevice() does, best-effort, before the play call lands. playUri now returns a SpotifyController.PlayOutcome instead of a bare Boolean, so a failed connect gets one of four distinct spoken lines (CouldNotFindSpotifyApp, NotLoggedInException, UserNotAuthorizedException, OfflineModeException) rather than one generic string, plus PlayRejected for a play() call that reached Spotify and was refused. The outcome -> message mapping and the connect-Throwable -> outcome mapping are both pure functions (SpotifyController.message/outcomeForConnectFailure), same shape as NavigationController's own outcome/message split, so they're covered by a plain-JVM test with no Context and no SDK connection. Also, per Kevin (2026-08-19): the foreground service now holds the App Remote connection itself (connectSilently in onCreate) instead of only ever connecting on the first voice command or from MainActivity.onResume. This deliberately violates Spotify's own documented guidance to connect in onStart and disconnect in onStop - the violation and the reason (latency on every utterance, in a car) are written into the code at both call sites so a future reader doesn't fix it back. Wires PlayerApi.subscribeToPlayerState() on every successful connect, exposed as SpotifyController.playerState (a StateFlow<PlayerState?>). Nothing reads it yet - tickets 07 and 09 do - and NowPlayingController's own reporting is deliberately unchanged in this ticket. Adds UserApi.getCapabilities().canPlayOnDemand as a best-effort, non-blocking check after a successful play: if it says the account can't play on demand, PlayOutcome.Started carries a spoken warning. Not a gate (this UX stays Premium-only by design) - it exists only so a non-Premium account is told in words instead of silently degraded. Does not touch SpotifyWebApi.kt's SCOPES list (owned by a parallel ticket on its own branch). Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Ticket 01 of the spotify-voice map (.scratch/spotify-voice/issues/01-scopes-and-one-reapproval.md). isAuthorized compares the granted scope string against SCOPES by exact equality, so adding a scope invalidates every existing grant and forces a browser re-approval - the one thing that cannot be done from the driver's seat. Widening SCOPES once per ticket across this whole map would mean up to nine separate re-approvals; this takes all nine scopes the map's settled decision table names in a single edit instead. - media/SpotifyWebApi.kt: SCOPES now also asks for user-modify-playback-state, user-read-playback-state, user-read-currently-playing, user-library-modify, playlist-read-private, playlist-read-collaborative, playlist-modify-private, playlist-modify-public, and app-remote-control, alongside the four scopes already held. Cross-checked against the map's decision table and research/01-api-capability-surface.md's capability listing before finishing - nothing there needs a scope not in this list. - ui/spotify/SpotifyConnectResolver.kt: rewrote REAUTHORIZATION_DETAIL_MESSAGE, which used to name three specific 2026-08-18 permissions by name. Keep the conversation when the socket dies, and say so when we cannot
no ticket
0e3319b · 4 files
Kevin, on a real drive: "after a few turns, it doesnt remember the previous turn what we said. the context drops." Gemini Live keeps history in the SOCKET, so anything that ends a socket ends the memory. The app resisted none of it: GeminiLiveSession.kt carried the comment "goAway / sessionResumptionUpdate are ignored in this version" while buildSetup requested neither resumption nor compression. The server has been telling us it was about to cut, and handing us the handle that would have let us continue, and we threw both away. Now: - buildSetup requests sessionResumption, sending the stored handle when there is one, and contextWindowCompression with a sliding window. - sessionResumptionUpdate is captured; a resumable handle is kept ON THE CONTROLLER, which is the whole point - it must outlive the session object it came from. - goAway is parsed for its timeLeft and we close DELIBERATELY a margin early, so the cutoff is a planned handover rather than a surprise abort. "goAway" joins NORMAL_CLOSE_REASONS so our own planned close never flashes CONNECTION LOST at the driver. Compression addresses a DIFFERENT ender than a network drop - the window filling - and is commented as such so nobody later mistakes it for the fix. THE HONESTY HALF, which was the actual bug. A resume that works says nothing; continuity is the expected case. A thread that could NOT be resumed now flashes "RECONNECTED - LOST TRACK OF WHAT WE WERE SAYING" and opens the next turn by telling the MODEL it does not remember, instead of beginConversation(null) answering cold. An assistant that has forgotten and does not say so is asserting a continuity it does not have - the same rule that put a facts prohibition in AriaBrain earlier tonight. A crisis teardown clears the handle too: that conversation must never silently resume. Transcript replay was rejected. It is turn-boundary text, not continuable session state, and replaying it risks the model reading old text as new driver speech. My own brief justified skipping it on the grounds that companion text is not captured; the executing agent checked and CORRECTED me - subtitles = true is hardcoded now (:492, "a core UX surface, not debug-only"), so companion text IS stored. The conclusion stands on the better reason, not the stale one. Protocol fields were fetched from ai.google.dev/api/live and grepped, not recalled: sessionResumption.handle, sessionResumptionUpdate.newHandle/resumable, goAway.timeLeft, contextWindowCompression.slidingWindow. UNPROVEN, and neither is small: no real goAway timeLeft has ever been observed, so the 3s margin is a guess with a comment saying so; and the protocol gives no ack for a rejected or expired handle, so "handle present means resume worked" is the best signal available, not a confirmation. Reproduce without a car: adb shell cmd connectivity airplane-mode enable, wait for the socket to die mid-conversation, disable, then tap. Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

It ends when he ends it (tapping the strip - onTap's `inConversation -> stop()`), when the socket dies (which already flashes CONNECTION LOST and returns the strip to a persistent "Tap to talk"), or on the crisis path. Any timer left armed by an earlier turn is cancelled so a stale one cannot fire mid-chat. armIdleTimeout now governs speak-only sessions only, which is its one remaining caller: vadMode false, no mic open, nothing to keep warm for. Two tests were red on this branch. They were not the same kind of problem. ProactiveBusTest > blocked while onboarding is incomplete was a REAL DEFECT. OnboardingState.isComplete delegated to GeminiKeyProvider.hasKey(), which deliberately falls back to BuildConfig.GEMINI_API_KEY so a convenience dev build does not need a key re-entered by hand. That fallback is correct for "what key do we call Gemini with" and wrong for "did the driver finish setup". On any local build with a real key in local.properties the gate silently stopped gating: clearing the on-file key still left onboarding reading complete, so ProactiveBus.speakIfAllowed no longer blocked. A distributed build ships -Pnokey and an empty field, so the two checks already agreed there - only the dev build diverged, which is why this hid. isComplete now reads CompanionProfile.geminiKey directly. GeminiKeyProvider is unchanged; the fallback still serves the call sites that need a usable key. Consequence on a dev build with a baked-in key: no prewarm and no proactive speech until a key is saved once through ui/KeyScreen.kt. BioDigestBuilderTest > bodyweight reports a weekly average was the TEST's fault - a fixture anchored 2 days back crosses the Monday boundary when the suite runs on a Monday or Tuesday, so the second reading fell into the previous week and the average came out 180.0 instead of 181.0. Anchored to weekStartEpoch(now) instead. `now` itself stays wall-clock because BioDigestBuilder anchors "today"/"this week" the same way; pinning it broke two other tests in the file. Full suite green, 1555 tests, verified with --rerun rather than a cached up-to-date result. Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

The master switch could not be honoured: three separate authors each hand-rolled their own checks, and the copies disagreed - neither bypasser checked onboarding-complete, so both could speak over first-run setup. The ticket's own premise said two paths ignored mute; traced, both did check it. What was broken is that nothing enforced it. ProactiveBus is the choke point now, with its documented objection answered rather than overridden. The reason it was not one was good: the DtcSheet ASK button is a button the driver just pressed and a mute must never silence it. The problem was one undifferentiated requestSpeak, so it splits by who asked - speakSolicited, never gated, and speakIfAllowed, the only unsolicited path. The raw emit is private, so bypass is impossible rather than merely unused. Found and fixed on the way in: handleState set isInCall before announcing the ringing call. Harmless while the announcement hand-rolled its checks; the moment it routed through a gate that checks isInCall, it would have blocked itself every time, silently, forever. That is the argument for a choke point in miniature - three copies of a rule hid an ordering dependency none of them stated. Kevin's calls: an incoming-call announcement IS proactive speech and the switch silences it, refusing the first candidate exemption to "nothing is exempt"; mute keeps stopping the microphone, not just speech; and ambient chatter is retired. speakQuietLine goes, both branches - including the offer to run through the list, which is list-aware but not due-aware. Speech triggered by the absence of conversation is the nearest thing here to a mechanism engineered to produce engagement. The first-meeting greeting raise goes; the flag write beside it stays, because the avatar-tap greeting reads it. Untested, stated rather than hidden: speakIfAllowed's in-call branch. isInCall is private set, written only from a real PhoneStateListener callback, and reflection would have manufactured coverage rather than earned it. Stop an ask_<domain> loop from claiming a write that never ran
no ticket
f97e1d8 · 4 files
Measured on-device: a driver spoke workout sets during a real 21:42-21:45 voice session. workout_set_logs has no row from that night, yet the app told him it was recorded. Logcat for the window proves log_workout_set was never dispatched at all - the driver's request went into ask_goals, whose investigate loop called only list_goals/ask_advisor (read tools) and still answered with prose the old code spoke verbatim as success = true. Root cause, traced two layers deep: - SubAgent.kt's investigate loop returned AgentResult.Success for ANY round that came back with zero functionCalls, with no memory of what actually ran - a sub-agent's prose alone could claim an action happened. - LiveToolbox.agentResult mapped every AgentResult.Success straight to result(true, ...), so that unchecked prose reached the driver as fact. - Compounding: the forced-answer round set functionCallingConfig.mode = "NONE", so a loop that had spent its whole budget on reads was physically unable to call a write tool even if it tried on its last round. What changed: 1. SubAgent.investigate gains mutatingToolNames: Set<String> = emptySet() (default keeps every existing caller byte-identical). The loop tracks, in its own local state - never MidnightEvents - which of those names actually got dispatched, and returns them as AgentResult.Success.mutatingToolsCalled: List<String> (also defaulted, so ask/askTyped/askWithUsage are unaffected). 2. LiveToolbox.MUTATING_TOOLS: an explicit, named set of every dispatch() branch that writes to Room or actuates real hardware (log_*/set_*/ create_*/manage_*/clear_pending_transaction/undo_last_log/tag_place/ forget_place/register_vehicle/remember/accept_proposal/activate_garage/ categorize_transactions/close_goal), enumerated from the real branches rather than inferred from a prefix at call time - deliberately excludes the five ask_<domain> dispatchers themselves (a router isn't a write) and the three UI-scoped hand-offs (dispatch() writes nothing for them). mutatingToolsFor(domain) intersects this with DISPATCHED[domain], so each ask_<domain> call passes investigate() only the mutating names actually reachable in that domain's own tool set. 3. LiveToolbox.agentResult gains requireMutation: Boolean = false and routes AgentResult.Success through the new pure successOrMutationRefusal (extracted the same way LiveSessionController.shouldRestoreAfterToolCall was, for unit coverage with no network/Room/Robolectric): when requireMutation is true and mutatingToolsCalled is empty, the sub-agent's text is discarded entirely and a plain "not recorded" refusal is spoken instead - never the false "logged it" that caused this. 4. The forced-answer trap: functionCallingConfig.mode = "NONE" now only fires on round maxModelCalls + 1, not maxModelCalls. Make SubAgent's HTTP round-trip actually cancellable
no ticket
854406f · 1 file
postOnce was a plain (non-suspend) HttpURLConnection call invoked from the suspend postRaw. Coroutine cancellation is cooperative, and a thread blocked inside Java socket I/O has no cooperation point to check - it only notices cancellation once the read returns on its own. That made every timeout above it inert: AgentTool.timeoutMs wrapping tool.run, investigate's own budgetMs, and LiveSessionController.handleToolCall's 45s withTimeoutOrNull for SUB_AGENT_TOOLS. The real ceiling was connectTimeout 15s / readTimeout 30s per attempt, times postRaw's one retry - enough for "log a bunch of meals" (routed through ask_body -> SubAgent.investigate as of 2a1c18e) to leave the UI on "Listening..." for minutes while a cancelled call kept running anyway. postOnce is now `private suspend fun postOnce(...) = withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { ... }`. Two things make cancellation real rather than cosmetic: 1. withContext(Dispatchers.IO) makes this suspend point itself cancellable. When the surrounding job is cancelled, withContext rethrows CancellationException at ITS OWN boundary as the call unwinds - not inside the block, so the block's `catch (e: Exception)` (which CancellationException is technically a subtype of) never gets a chance to swallow it. Traced: postRaw's retry loop only re-enters ("attempt == 0" -> delay -> continue) if postOnce RETURNS a value; on cancellation postOnce never returns to postRaw at all, it propagates the cancellation through the suspend call, so the loop cannot retry a cancelled attempt. No extra isActive guard needed - this is withContext's own contract, not an assumption. 2. `coroutineContext.job.invokeOnCompletion` registers a callback that calls connection.disconnect() the moment this coroutine's job completes for any non-null cause (i.e. cancellation). That's what actually unblocks the thread parked in outputStream/responseCode/ inputStream - without it, withContext's own cancellation check only fires when the blocking call eventually returns on its own, i.e. never before the socket's own 30s read timeout. The handle is disposed in the existing finally alongside connection.disconnect(), so a normal completion cleans it up as a no-op and a cancelled one as a fired one - either order is harmless. connectTimeout/readTimeout values are untouched; they remain the backstop for a stall under no caller timeout at all, not the thing actually bounding a stuck call anymore. Traced: grepped all callers of postOnce/postRaw inside SubAgent.kt - postRaw has exactly four callers (ask, askWithUsage, askTyped, runInvestigation), all already suspend funs; postOnce has exactly one caller (postRaw). No non-coroutine entry point exists that this change could break. Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Resolve the scheduling research, and correct two premises I got wrong
proactive-mode 07
8f8d643 · 3 files
Both errors were mine, in the brief. The app targets SDK 34, not 36 - the A25 runs Android 16, which is a different thing entirely - so the six-hour dataSync cap, the BOOT_COMPLETED foreground-service block and the global DND lockout are all dormant today and armed only by a targetSdk bump that sideloading means nothing forces. And I cited MEMORY as establishing Samsung OEM aggression on this phone; the file actually attributes that adb failure to Git Bash path mangling and has no pm clear entry at all. The research rebuilt that section on Samsung's own documentation instead of my misreading. The threat turns out not to be the cap I sent it looking for. Samsung's own sleeping-apps layer puts an app unused for around three days into a restricted bucket - one alarm per day, no network - while the foreground service keeps running and everything looks healthy. A voice assistant used daily without its UI ever being opened is precisely that profile, which is what LEGION is. Also found: on Android 16, applying already at target 34, jobs running concurrently with a foreground service now obey the runtime quota, so the service no longer buys unlimited WorkManager time. AriaForegroundService uses dataSync as its base type because it is the only type with no runtime prerequisite, and it is the only one with a kill timer; neither it nor LedgerIngestService implements onTimeout, so the eventual failure is a fatal RemoteServiceException rather than degradation. And no app-only DND bypass exists at any importance or category, which bounds what may ever speak during quiet hours. Recommendations are recorded but not acted on: dropping dataSync changes foreground service behaviour and is a decision for the delivery ticket, not something to do unattended at night. Ten items need the phone, and they have one gate: whether the service survives a twelve-hour screen-off unplugged run at all. Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

35c4929 · 3 files
The bug was never fixed, only latched around: rekeyExistingRows still blind UPDATEd a row into a duplicate when the destination identity already existed, and what stopped it on Kevin's phone was completed_v3 latching after 17 colliding rows were deleted by hand. Any device that has not latched still carries it, the retired A17k included. The first attempt at this hung on the device and was reverted to a stash. The ticket blamed concurrent sync-writer contention. The likelier cause is duller: obd_samples has no index at all beyond its primary key, and that attempt still issued one UPDATE or DELETE per bundle row - up to 11,511 - each with a WHERE over pid, timestamp and vehicleId. That is eleven thousand full table scans over a table holding up to 36,694 rows, on a table this very bug inflates. It fits the symptom without needing contention to explain it. So the apply step is now set-based: bucket candidates in memory against the identity set already loaded once, then one DELETE and one UPDATE per table per move, matched against a temp table. Worst case becomes a few scans of the table rather than one scan per row. A source row is deleted only when its full identity already exists at the destination, which is what makes deletion safe rather than lossy, and the identity columns are named per table on the ticket. Four repeated passes converge to one row. The honest limit: this cannot run on Kevin's phone at all, because his import is latched complete. Exercising it needs a device with completed_v3 unset, a colliding bundle present, and enough obd_samples volume to reproduce the timing. So it ships as code that compiles, passes 1474 tests, and has never run against the condition it exists for. Flagged and not built: obd_samples probably wants an index on vehicleId, pid and timestamp. It is the biggest table, it is what this hang scanned repeatedly, and the faults drilldown now range-queries it per event row. Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Stop mail reaching permanent memory through remember
google-account-integration 21
fa11936 · 5 files
The read-through rule says mail is read, used and dropped. The episodic path enforced it well - it discards the entire turn, flagged when the tool call arrives rather than after dispatch, because turnComplete can land first. But remember was not gated on that flag at all and writes MemoryEntry directly. So Alfred read an email, the driver said "remember that", and the content became permanent, while the turn that would have recorded where it came from was correctly thrown away. The write survived; its provenance did not. remember now refuses in a turn that touched a read-through tool: "I don't keep anything from mail - that's on purpose, not a slip. Tell me the fact yourself, in your own words, and I'll remember that." The cost is real and is on the ticket: Alfred cannot remember a fact the driver just learned from an email, even asked directly. Whether an explicit human ask is a valid exception, as the garage precedent would suggest, is answered no for now and reverses in one line. Gated on membership in EPISODIC_EXCLUDED_TOOLS, never on the two literal tool names, because that set is the map's stated precedent for every future read-through sense and gating on names would silently reopen this for each one. A test adds a fake name to the set and asserts it also blocks. Checked for a second route and found none: the consolidator reads only episodic turns, which are already dropped whole on a mail turn, and reflection reads only already-consolidated memories, one hop further downstream. Reported rather than quietly widened. Also fixed the smaller sibling from the same ticket. search_mail's query rode the payload with a comment saying "so Alfred always has it to say" while nothing ever asked him to say it. The instruction is now in the tool's own description. 1442 tests green. What is deliberately left open: nobody has audited what may already be sitting in memory from before today, and only Kevin can recognise a memory that came from an email.
